facts.text: Start an incident log, `~/{{incidentDir}}/{{incidentLog}}`, with the computer's IP address and the address of the gateway.
facts.hint: `ip a` shows the address and `ip route` the gateway (the line `default via`). Send the output to the log with `>` and `>>`.

ping-out.text: Show that the network works all the way out to the internet – name lookups included. Add a ping with three packets to a name on the internet to the log.
ping-out.hint: Ping a **name**, not an address, and you test DNS too: `ping -c 3 example.com`, and finish with `>>`.

listening.text: The website is myserver on port 8080. Find out whether anything is listening on the port – and if nothing is, start the web server and check again.
listening.hint: `ss -tulpn` shows the listening ports. If 8080 is missing, start the server with `myserver` (or with `systemctl`).

headers.text: Does the website answer as it should? Add the response headers of the front page, `http://localhost:8080`, to the log. The status code should be 200.
headers.hint: `curl -I` fetches only the headers. On Ubuntu, curl has to be installed first: `sudo apt install curl`.

key.text: Next time you want to get into the server `server.lan` without a password. Create a key pair and put the public key on the server.
key.hint: `ssh-keygen` creates the key pair – press Enter at the questions. `ssh-copy-id` then puts the public key on the server, for example `ssh-copy-id srv`.

backup.text: Back up the whole folder `~/{{incidentDir}}` to your home directory on the server, so that the log is still there even if your computer gives up.
backup.hint: `rsync -av` with a slash after the source copies the contents: `rsync -av ~/{{incidentDir}}/ srv:{{incidentDir}}/`. `scp -r` works too.

remote-read.text: Show the log that is on the server with `ssh` – without anyone asking for a password.
remote-read.hint: Write the command after the host: `ssh srv cat {{incidentDir}}/{{incidentLog}}`. If ssh asks for a password, the key is not in place.
